entries.clue: Two descriptions of freshly-baked cake that’s finished off? (4,3,6)

blocks.note: the surface reading: a baker's two words for a cake out of the oven, one for cooked through and one for sprinkled with icing sugar
the setter's reading: join those two baking words with 'and' and you have a stock phrase for a job completely finished

annotation.surface: A baker describing a cake fresh out of the oven.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads the idiom literally: two baking words joined by AND, which together mean completely finished.
annotation.definitionFit: Done and dusted is the everyday British phrase for a task completely finished.

entries.clue: Morning’s fresh water and powder sprinkled around duke (7)

indicatorNotes.sprinkled: powder that is sprinkled is scattered, so its letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.around: the rearranged letters go around the D

blocks.note: POWDER rearranged, split as DEW…ROP
D = duke, placed after DEW

annotation.surface: A dawn scene, with talc scattered about a nobleman.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: a dewdrop is the water freshly formed in the morning.
annotation.definitionFit: A dewdrop is a bead of moisture that forms overnight and is seen fresh in the morning.

entries.clue: Report of Bishop’s neighbour’s darkest hours (5)

indicatorNotes.Report of: a report is something spoken, so what follows is to be said out loud

blocks.note: on a chessboard the knight starts next to the bishop

annotation.surface: A newspaper report on the dark times of a bishop's neighbour.
annotation.walkthrough: Bishop looks like a churchman, but here it is the chess piece; its neighbour on the back rank is the knight.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the hours between dusk and dawn are the darkest of the day.

entries.clue: Agrees, in a hearing, say, to be heard (7)

indicatorNotes.to be heard: tells you to take the sound of the words, not their spelling

blocks.note: hearing is one example of a sense, so 'a hearing, say' = A SENSE

annotation.surface: Someone agreeing to something at a court hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' looks like a court session; it is the sense of hearing, and 'say' marks it as one example of a sense.
annotation.definitionFit: To assent is to agree, so 'assents' = 'agrees'.

entries.clue: Moving round Asia – and El Dorado! – showing no animation (4,2,1,8)

indicatorNotes.Moving round: letters moving round are shifted about into new places

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

annotation.surface: An explorer travelling round Asia and the fabled golden city, oddly unexcited.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pairs a journey with a lack of excitement; the fifteen letters of the place names make the idiom for lifeless.
annotation.definitionFit: Something dead as a doornail shows no life or movement at all.

entries.clue: Removes ropes from a French doctor, son (6)

blocks.note: un = a in French
to doctor results is to rig them
S = son

annotation.surface: Sailors stripping the rigging from a French doctor and his son.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is a verb here, meaning to falsify, not a physician.
annotation.definitionFit: To unrig a ship is to take down its ropes and tackle.

entries.clue: Customs planting Detective Inspector in time-share (9)

annotation.definitionNote: plural 'customs' against singular TRADITION, read as a body of customs

indicatorNotes.in: the DI goes in the other letters

blocks.note: T = time
a ration is a share; DI goes between RA and TION
DI = Detective Inspector

annotation.surface: Customs officers planting a detective in a holiday time-share.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Customs' suggests the border service, and 'time-share' a holiday property; split it into time and share.
annotation.definitionFit: Tradition is the body of customs handed down within a group.

entries.clue: Furniture item as’ll help actor (7)

blocks.note: a kitchen sideboard with shelves for crockery above
a backstage theatre job: the person who helps an actor into costume

annotation.surface: A piece of furniture that will lend an actor a hand.
annotation.walkthrough: 'As'll' is a folksy 'as will' joining the two senses: the furniture and the backstage helper.
annotation.definitionFit: A dresser is both a shelved cupboard and a person who dresses actors.

entries.clue: Suddenly realise: t-toupée! (4)

blocks.note: the stammered first letter
a toupée is a small wig

annotation.surface: Someone stammering in shock as they realise another person's hair is a toupée.
annotation.walkthrough: The stutter is the wordplay: T followed by the hairpiece. Twig is British slang for suddenly understanding.
annotation.definitionFit: To twig is British slang for suddenly grasping or realising something.

entries.clue: Flights, not all ending in landings? (10)

annotation.definition: Flights, not all ending in landings?

blocks.note: the surface reading is air travel; the setter means flights of stairs
planes should all land, but a flight of stairs may or may not reach a landing at the top

annotation.surface: Air travel, with the worry that not every flight ends in a safe touchdown.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flights' and 'landings' suggest aircraft; both are also parts of a staircase.
annotation.definitionFit: A flight is a run of stairs, and a staircase may or may not end in a landing.

entries.clue: Particle; Rutherford originated this one’s name, orginally! (6)

annotation.definition: Particle; Rutherford originated this one’s name, orginally!

indicatorNotes.orginally: a misspelling of 'originally': take the first letter of each word

blocks.clueFragment: Particle; Rutherford originated this one’s name
blocks.note: first letters of Particle, Rutherford, Originated, This, One's, Name

annotation.surface: A physics fact: Ernest Rutherford gave the proton its name.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the letter source; it is also true, since Rutherford named the proton in 1920.
annotation.definitionFit: The &lit reads straight: this nuclear particle really was named by Ernest Rutherford, around 1920.

entries.clue: Rashly tasering Tangiers’ ingrates, picking any that’s most furious? (8)

indicatorNotes.Rashly: letters handled rashly are thrown about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters; TANGIERS and INGRATES have the same letters, so 'picking any' lets you use whichever you like
two more words with the same eight letters, offered as alternative fodder; 'picking any' says one of the three will do

annotation.surface: Police rashly tasering ungrateful people in Tangiers, trying to find the angriest.
annotation.walkthrough: TASERING, TANGIERS and INGRATES are all anagrams of ANGRIEST; 'picking any' tells you to use any one of them.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the superlative: angry and furious are near-equivalents, and both clue and answer take the 'most' form.

entries.clue: As a report misrepresented Pavarotti? (5,4)

annotation.definitionNote: Pavarotti is an example of an opera star, signalled by the '?'

indicatorNotes.misrepresented: the letters are presented wrongly, in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A news report that misrepresented the famous tenor.
annotation.walkthrough: Pavarotti is a definition by example, which the question mark flags.
annotation.definitionFit: Luciano Pavarotti was one of the best-known opera stars.

entries.clue: The cigars distributed in Parliament (9)

indicatorNotes.distributed: letters distributed are handed out in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: Cigars being handed round in the House of Commons.
annotation.walkthrough: The Reichstag is the German parliament, and its building in Berlin.
annotation.definitionFit: The Reichstag was Germany's parliament and still names its parliament building.

entries.clue: Deceiver in bar rebuffed (4)

indicatorNotes.rebuffed: something rebuffed is pushed back, so read it backwards

blocks.note: a rail is a bar

annotation.surface: A con man in a pub being turned away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub; it is a rail.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who tells untruths is deceiving the listener, though a deceiver need not use words.

entries.clue: On reflection, fan – Everyman admitted – is … not a sophisticated type (4)

indicatorNotes.admitted: someone admitted is let in through the door, so the setter's I goes inside the other letters

blocks.note: turned back to NAF
the setter refers to himself as I, placed inside NA…F

annotation.surface: A remark that a fan who got in to see Everyman is a bit unworldly.
annotation.walkthrough: When a setter names himself, as Everyman does here, he usually stands for I or ME.
annotation.definitionFit: A naif is a naive, unsophisticated person.

entries.clue: Earned around half a C; caused irritation (7)

indicatorNotes.around: 'around' places the word for earned on either side of the letter, enclosing it

blocks.note: to net a sum is to earn it; the L goes between NETT and ED
in Roman numerals C = 100 and L = 50

annotation.surface: Someone earning around fifty pounds and feeling annoyed about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half a C' looks like a letter to split, but it is arithmetic in Roman numerals: half of 100 is 50, L.
annotation.definitionFit: Nettled means irritated, like the sting of a nettle; here 'caused irritation' reads as 'irritated'.

entries.clue: Contemptuous quality, characteristic of nit? (9)

blocks.note: lousy = rotten, contemptible
a nit is a louse's egg, so being 'lousy' in the literal sense

annotation.surface: An insult: sneering is typical of a nitwit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nit' looks like the insult for a fool; it is the egg of a louse, taken literally.
annotation.definitionFit: Lousiness is the quality of being lousy, i.e. poor or contemptible.

entries.clue: Drunkenly wails welcoming greeting – language! (7)

indicatorNotes.Drunkenly: letters behaving drunkenly stagger out of order
indicatorNotes.welcoming: a host welcoming a guest takes them inside, so the rearranged letters take the greeting in

blocks.note: WAILS rearranged, split SWA…LI
hi = a greeting

annotation.surface: A drunk wailing a greeting and being told off for swearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Language!' is the scold for swearing; here it is the definition, Swahili.
annotation.definitionFit: Swahili is a language widely spoken in East Africa.

entries.clue: Hide, in part of Mediterranean island closest to Cairo (7)

blocks.note: the part is the south-eastern part
Cairo lies south-east of Crete, so SE = the south-east
the Greek island of Crete

annotation.surface: Someone hiding out in the corner of a Mediterranean island nearest Egypt.
annotation.walkthrough: SE CRETE is the south-east part of Crete, the part nearest Cairo in Egypt.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of stashing away, not the biological sense of producing a fluid.

entries.clue: Demur, having a thing (6)

blocks.note: a verb: to raise a protest or doubt
a noun: any physical item

annotation.surface: Someone raising an objection because they have a thing about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The verb and the noun share a spelling but not a stress: obJECT against OBject.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain synonyms of different parts of speech: the verb for protesting and the noun for an item.

entries.clue: Here you may see advocate – or advocaat (2,3,3)

annotation.definitionNote: each is where the thing is found, 'here you may see', rather than a synonym

blocks.note: an advocate is a lawyer who pleads in court; barristers practise in the profession called the bar
advocaat is a Dutch egg liqueur, served at a pub bar

annotation.surface: A near-spelling joke: the lawyer and the liqueur found in the same place.
annotation.walkthrough: The two words differ by one letter; 'the bar' is both the legal profession and a counter serving drinks.
annotation.definitionFit: A barrister is called to the bar; a drink is served at the bar.

entries.clue: Pacino’s stunning in Somewhere in France (6)

blocks.note: Al Pacino, the actor
the 's kept as S
ace = excellent, stunning

annotation.surface: A review saying Al Pacino is stunning in a film called Somewhere in France.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Somewhere in France' look like a film title; it is the definition, a French region.
annotation.definitionFit: Alsace is a region in north-east France.

entries.clue: Dish – often fish, portion of Hippoglossus hippoglossus (5)

indicatorNotes.portion of: the answer is a portion of the words that follow

blocks.note: hippogloSSUS HIppoglossus

annotation.surface: A dish of fish, part of it halibut, given by its Latin name.
annotation.walkthrough: Hippoglossus hippoglossus is the scientific name of the Atlantic halibut, itself used in sushi.
annotation.definitionFit: Sushi is a Japanese dish of rice often topped with raw fish.

entries.clue: Glamorous types’ bit of glam rubbish at #1? (10)

indicatorNotes.bit of: take just the first bit of the word

blocks.note: the first letter of glam
litter = rubbish
kept as written
I = one, the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: Celebrities' glamorous rubbish topping the charts at number one.
annotation.walkthrough: '#1' suggests a chart-topper; it is one, the Roman I.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word blends glitter with literati to mean the fashionable celebrity set.

entries.clue: That woman had place to keep tools (4)

blocks.note: she = that woman
had is contracted to an apostrophe and D after a pronoun

annotation.surface: A woman who had somewhere to store her tools.
annotation.walkthrough: SHE'D is 'she had' contracted; drop the apostrophe and it is SHED.
annotation.definitionFit: A shed is a garden hut where tools are kept.

entries.clue: Modern inequality, focus of flip-flop? (7,6)

blocks.note: the setter's reading: the gap between people with and without computers and internet access
the surface reading is the sandal: its post splits the toes, which are digits

annotation.surface: Asking what a sandal is really about.
annotation.walkthrough: Digital means of fingers and toes as well as of computers; the post of a flip-flop divides the big toe from the rest, and a flip-flop is also a binary circuit.
annotation.definitionFit: The digital divide is the gap between those with and without internet and computer access.
